title: Concentrations of IL-6 in Saliva and Serum in Comparison with Salivary Amylase and Clinical Indicators of Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria
content: Background and Objectives: Although the diagnosis of chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) is primarily clinical, detailed history taking and selected laboratory findings are important for patient evaluation and management. Materials and Methods: This explorative prospective study included 41 CSU patients who were followed for 3 months during antihistamine treatment. Saliva and blood samples were collected, and disease-related questionnaires were completed at baseline (T1) and at follow-up (T2). Salivary IL-6 and amylase, serum IL-6, and standard laboratory parameters, including differential blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and/or C-reactive protein (CRP), total IgE, TSH, T4, and anti-TPO antibodies, were measured and compared with disease activity (UAS7), disease control (UCT), and quality of life (DLQI and CU-Q2oL). Results: Salivary IL-6 showed a weak correlation with serum CRP. Neither salivary nor serum IL-6 showed a consistent association with CSU severity, disease control, or quality-of-life scores. Serum IL-6 showed significant correlations with selected inflammatory and thyroid-related parameters. Salivary IL-6 values at baseline (T1) were more frequently increased in patients experiencing a major disease impact on quality of life (CU-Q2oL-measured) than in those with a moderate impact on CU-specific quality of life. Also, higher salivary IL-6 values were expressed in patients with uncontrolled CSU than in well-controlled CSU, as measured by the UCT questionnaire, although without significant difference between these parameters. Conclusions: Salivary IL-6 showed a weak correlation with CRP, but no consistent association with CSU clinical features. Salivary IL-6 is of exploratory interest, but larger controlled studies are needed before any clinical utility can be inferred.
